A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, algorithms, equations, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports theoretical guarantees and proofs, but no original empirical results. Its tables summarize notation and theoretical runtimes.

after.justification: Appendix K reports three original synthetic experiments, with measured runtimes and errors in Tables 4–6.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 introduce a sparsity-aware adaptation that solves weighted regressions using the nonzero support of the weights. The alternating updates, preconditioned regression solver, clipping and QR procedures otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual evaluations on synthetic noisy matrix completion, dense weighted low-rank approximation and standalone least-squares regression. These cover Gaussian, Laplace and uniform matrix factors, plus power-law regression data; v2 contains no empirical evaluation.

E2.justification: Tables 4–5 newly evaluate the proposed algorithm against the exact alternating-minimization solver from LLR16. Table 6 adds an exact regression-solver comparison. LLR16 appeared only in theoretical comparisons in v2.

E3.justification: Appendix K introduces experimental protocols: n=800, k=100, CountSketch size 150 and 20 alternating iterations for the matrix experiments; n=10^6, k=500, sketch size 5500 and five iterations for regression. It reports execution times and explicitly defines solution infinity-norm error for regression. These are new protocols, not revisions of existing experiments.

E4.justification: Experiment 3 adds a focused study of the regression subroutine, motivated by whether acceleration increases when n greatly exceeds k. This provides limited component-level evidence; the different task and single configuration do not establish a controlled end-to-end scaling analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. The theoretical failure probabilities are not experimental uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 4–6 add previously absent numerical results. Reported speedups are 12.39%–16.53% for matrix completion, 2.71%–10.84% for weighted approximation and 19.27%–29.45% for regression. Every matrix-experiment row reports higher error for the approximate solver than for the exact solver.

T1.justification: The runtime theorems replace n^2k with nnz(W)k, supported by a new support-size argument. The SRHT embedding row bound changes from log(n/delta) to log^2(n/delta). Most convergence proofs are retained, but new Lemma 4.5 gives an inverse-first-power incoherence bound where v2 Lemma E.8 and v3 Appendix D.9 use inverse-square dependence.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion strengthen the central efficiency claim from dense-matrix dependence to dependence on the number of nonzero weights. The near-verification-time interpretation consequently extends to sparse weights. The central claim of robust approximate alternating minimization is retained.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive justifications of the recovery assumptions, discusses rectangular-matrix applicability and interprets anticipated speedups for large n/k. The conclusion replaces v2's discussion of approximate QR as an unresolved limitation with emphasis on cubic SVD initialization. Appendix K adds computational limits and interpretations of the timing/error results.

D1.justification: Appendix K adds synthetic-data generation rules, factor scaling, noise variance, weight construction, sketch choices and iteration budgets. These provide limited reproducibility guidance beyond the retained pseudocode; hardware, software, code access and the matrix experiments' error metric remain unspecified.

R1.justification: New Section 4.4 substantially expands positioning against noisy and noiseless matrix-completion methods and nonconvex-landscape research. The introduction adds BRW21 and Dai23, while Appendix B broadens the sketching literature. GSYZ23 becoming GSYZ24 is a publication update, but its substantive comparison is expanded.

P1.justification: v3 extensively reorganizes and rewrites the exposition: expanded preliminaries, a unified results section, new explanations of the convergence argument, and a rewritten conclusion. Regression and subspace material move between the main text and reorganized appendices, and a contents list is added.

P2.justification: v3 adds three experimental result tables and an expanded main-text presentation of the existing notation table. It retains the appendix notation and runtime tables under new numbers, simplifies Algorithm 1 by removing analysis-only lines, and adds contents pages. These substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful organization, a sparsity argument, broader context and empirical timing evidence. However, Tables 4–5 do not specify their error metric, and Experiment 2's stated Gaussian-perturbed weights can violate nonnegativity without a documented correction. Theorem 4.6 omits the explicit small-gamma restriction still required by Lemma J.1, and new Lemma 4.5 conflicts with Appendix D.9's incoherence bound. These benefits and new consistency problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
